title: Proof pages for a recruiting firm
metaTitle: Proof pages for a recruiting firm
excerpt: Show the constraint, the decision, and the kind of role. A screenshot without a decision is decoration. End on how to brief a similar search.
alt: An open notebook with the word Notes underlined, a fountain pen, and glasses on a wooden desk, the page where a search decision should be written in sentences.
caption: A proof page should read like notes with a decision in them. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the opening of a recruiting proof page say?
faqs.answer: State the constraint, the decision, and the kind of role. The constraint is what made the search easy to get wrong. The decision needs a verb and a cost, such as refusing to widen a scorecard. The role should use the same words as the homepage so a hiring manager can tell whether the story matches their seat.

faqs.question: Can a firm publish proof without naming the client?
faqs.answer: Yes. Keep the role family, the company shape, and the decision, and drop the brand. Agree that boundary before you design the page. If the client will not allow the decision to be told, you have a logo rather than a proof page, so do not invent a result to fill the gap.

faqs.question: How should a recruiting case study end?
faqs.answer: Tell a similar buyer how to brief the search: the role, the constraint, and what the last attempt got wrong. One action is enough. Do not end by asking them to share their story, and do not promise a shortlist from a single paragraph.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A recruiting firm case study page should show a hiring manager who has been burned before three things: the constraint, the decision, and the kind of role you fill. A screenshot with no decision is decoration. End on how a similar buyer can brief the search. The Princeton GEO paper, by Aggarwal, Murahari, and colleagues, found that adding citations, quotations, and statistics raised source visibility by over 40 percent on their benchmark. A proof page full of mood and logos gives a person, and a generative engine, nothing solid to quote.

Write the page so a stranger can retell the decision without your help. If they can only retell that the client was delighted, you have written a compliment, not a proof.

## Constraint, decision, and the role

Open with the constraint in two sentences. What was true before you started, and what made the search easy to get wrong. A family-owned plant needed a manager who had run a night shift. The previous firm had widened the net until the slate was people who had managed spreadsheets, not a floor. The seat had been open for four months. Pick the facts that changed the work. Leave the rest in the file.

Then the decision. What you refused, what you insisted on, or what you changed in the scorecard. You refused to add "any operations leader" as an acceptable background. You insisted the hiring manager sit in the calibration before the first call. You stopped outreach for a week when the scorecard still had six priorities. A decision has a verb and a cost. "We partnered closely" has neither.

Then the kind of role, in the same words you use on the homepage. If this story is a plant-leadership search, say that in the first screen. A burned buyer is pattern-matching. They are asking whether your hard search looks like their hard search. A flattering story about a different role teaches them to look elsewhere. Put that story on its own page, under that role, or do not publish it.

Do not open with the client's praise. Praise is a closing line, and only if it refers to the decision. "They held the scorecard when the board wanted a familiar name" is praise with a decision inside it. "A true partner" is not.

## Why a screenshot is not a case

A cropped inbox, a redacted thread, or a slide of headshots does not show a decision. It shows that software was open. Nielsen Norman Group's research is a useful restraint: people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and they have time to read only about a quarter of the words on a page they do visit. If the first thing they see is a mosaic of interfaces, they will not dig the decision out of a caption.

Use a picture only when the picture is the decision. A scorecard with three criteria and the rejected fourth struck through, the role title visible. A shortlist of five redacted names beside the rule that the list would not grow. If you cannot show the artifact without exposing a candidate, describe it in two sentences. A description beats a blurred rectangle.

The same rule applies to a portrait of people shaking hands. That picture is the homepage mistake again. The proof page is not a second chance to run it. If you need a person in the frame, show them with the artifact: a marked-up scorecard, a debrief agenda, the office where the role is actually done. The scene should be checkable against the paragraph beside it.

Write the alt text as if the image failed to load and the sentence had to carry the point. "Team celebrating a placement" describes a party. "A one-page scorecard with the night-shift requirement circled" describes the proof.

## What you may tell

Confidential searches are not an excuse for an empty page. Change the names. Keep the constraint. A reader does not need the company's brand to learn that you will not widen a scorecard. They do need the role family, the company shape, and the decision. "A mid-size food manufacturer" is enough company. "A leading global brand" is fog.

Agree the boundary with the client before you draft, not after the page is designed. Ask what they will sign: role family, company shape, the decision, and a timeline with the season but not the announcement date. If they will not sign the decision, you do not have a proof page. You have a logo. Thank them and wait for a search you can tell.

Do not invent a result. If the person stayed a year, and you are allowed to say so, say so, and say how you know. If you do not know, stop at the decision and the shortlist rule. A made-up retention number is the kind of claim a burned buyer is hunting. The GEO finding about statistics is not an invitation to mint one. Use a real figure you can stand behind, or leave the number out and keep the decision sharp.

A useful number, if you have one you trust, is the size of the shortlist and how many weeks the search took. Those figures are checkable. A percentage gain in "quality of hire" is not, unless you can say how it was measured. A concrete figure gives a reader something to hold. It does not ask you to decorate the story with a metric from a slide. If the only number you trust is "five names, and we would not add a sixth," publish that and stop.

Candidates are not props. Do not publish a name, a photo, or a distinctive career path without permission. Redact more than feels necessary. A plant with one night shift in a small region can be identified from details you thought were generic. Read the draft the way a competitor would.

## How the page should end

The last section is for the buyer who recognized their own constraint. Tell them how to brief a similar search. What to send: the role title, the company shape, the constraint, and what the last attempt got wrong. What you will do next: say whether you take this kind of search, and what the first conversation covers. What you will not do: promise a shortlist from a paragraph.

One action. "Brief a search like this." The form should know which proof they came from, so your reply can refer to the same decision. A generic contact form at the end wastes the recognition you just earned.

Do not end on an invitation to "share your story." That asks them to perform. The brief asks them to hand you the constraint. Those are different requests. The second one is the point of the page.

If the fee shape matters to this kind of search, one sentence can name it. Do not paste the whole fee explanation under every story. The story's job is the decision. The fee has its own page.

## How many stories you need

Two or three stories are enough if each one contains a decision. Ten stories that all say the client was happy are a brochure. Publish the searches that match the offers on the services page. If you have no story yet for an offer, do not invent one. Leave the offer up only when the outcome and the boundary are already clear, and add the story when a client will let you tell the decision.

Date the page with the year of the search, or say it was a search from the last two years if a date would identify the client. Undated proof feels like it could belong to a previous firm. A burned buyer notices. Remove or rewrite a story when the method has changed. A page that describes a scorecard you no longer use is a promise you will be asked to keep.

Give each story its own address and a title that names the role and the decision. "Case study" does not say which search the page is about. "A plant-manager search we refused to widen" does. Do not reuse one boilerplate title and swap only a codename. A hiring manager scanning a list of proof should be able to pick the story that matches their seat without opening all of them.

## A drafting order that protects the decision

Write in this order, on one page, before any layout.

1. The constraint, in two sentences.
2. The decision, with a verb and a cost.
3. The role family, in homepage language.
4. What you will not disclose.
5. The brief: what a similar buyer should send.

Then read it to someone who was not on the search. If they cannot say what you refused, the decision is still missing. Add it. Do not add adjectives.

Only then choose a picture. If the picture does not show the constraint or the artifact, it does not go on the page. Layout is not how a weak story becomes proof. A quiet page with one decision will be quoted. A busy page with five impressions will not.

When the story can be retold, the buyer still has to find it. Read [how the navigation should name the search, not the department](/blog/navigation-for-a-recruiting-firm) so the proof sits on a path a hiring manager already understands.

If you want to pressure-test a proof page before it is public, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the constraint and the decision. Leave the adjectives in the draft you are willing to cut.
